red_flags: Fever with rigors, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain (Charcot's triad) — ascending cholangitis; urgent surgical referral
The above plus hypotension or confusion — suppurative cholangitis
Rigid abdomen with generalized rebound — perforation (gallbladder or ulcer); urgent surgical referral
Swinging high fever with a tender enlarged liver — liver abscess at risk of rupture
Persistent vomiting with signs of dehydration and no urine output
exam: Record temperature, BP, and pulse — sepsis pattern points to cholangitis or abscess
Inspect sclera in daylight for jaundice
Elicit Murphy's sign — arrest of inspiration on right subcostal pressure
Palpate for a tender gallbladder mass below the right costal margin
Palpate the liver edge — tender smooth hepatomegaly suggests hepatitis or abscess
Press over the right lower intercostal spaces — point tenderness supports liver abscess
Percuss and auscultate the right lung base — dullness or crackles point to basal pneumonia
Palpate the epigastrium separately — maximal epigastric tenderness shifts suspicion to ulcer or pancreatitis
Look for stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider nevi, palmar erythema)
Assess hydration and check for signs of shock

investigations.why: First-line and decisive: stones with a thickened gallbladder wall and sonographic Murphy's rules in cholecystitis; a dilated common bile duct supports choledocholithiasis/cholangitis; a hypoechoic liver lesion rules in abscess
Normal count fits uncomplicated biliary colic; leukocytosis supports cholecystitis, cholangitis, or liver abscess
Obstructive pattern (raised ALP and bilirubin) supports duct stone or cholangitis; transaminases in the thousands rule in acute hepatitis over the surgical causes
Rules acute pancreatitis in or out — gallstone pancreatitis sits in the same population as biliary colic
High values separate inflammatory disease (cholecystitis, abscess, pneumonia) from pure colic and dyspepsia

investigations.test: Viral hepatitis serology (HBsAg, anti-HCV, HAV IgM)
investigations.why: Confirms acute viral hepatitis when LFT shows a hepatitic rather than obstructive pattern
Supports amebic liver abscess when ultrasound shows a liver collection with a dysentery history
Right basal consolidation rules in pneumonia as the referred cause; free air under the diaphragm rules in perforated ulcer
Second-line — if the duct is dilated on ultrasound but no stone is seen, or a liver lesion needs characterization before referral
